<Rep. Robert Garcia>: The Minority strongly opposes H.R. 1507, a bill to repeal the Comprehensive Policing and Justice Reform Amendment Act of 2022 enacted by the District of Columbia Council. This radical measure seeks to nullify the duly enacted laws of the District of Columbia and violates the very heart of the democratic principles on which our nation is based.
It is not the place of Congress--which is not accountable to D.C. residents--to micromanage the District and act as some kind of super legislature, second-guessing their laws.
Like many cities around the country, the District of Columbia passed police reform packages in 2020. The D.C. police reform legislation aimed at accountability for police officers who use excessive force or abuse their power. It increased transparency and provided stronger civilian oversight. And it empowers the chief of police to punish officer misconduct and criminal activity, including by firing officers. It set reasonable standards for the use of deadly force.
The D.C. law also prohibited the hiring of police officers with prior misconduct charges. It established education and training requirements to address racism, biased policing, and white supremacy.
In the wake of the killing of George Floyd, similar policies were passed in communities all over the country as communities worked to restore trust between police and residents and to address past injustices. This bill seeks to undo all of that. The first draft of this bill even tried to repeal a ban on dangerous chokeholds and neck restraints by police officers.
H.R. 5107 rejects mainstream, commonsense reforms, which are consistent with police accountability laws enacted by dozens of states and localities in recent years.
For example, since May of 2020, at least 24 states have enacted legislation to limit the use of neck restraints. 39 states have passed reforms related to officer education and training requirements. 26 states have enacted laws to improve data collection and increase transparency in policing. At least seven states, including Arizona, Colorado, and Wisconsin, have enacted legislation requiring the creation of public databases on use-of-force information. States like Colorado, South Carolina and Maryland have mandated adoption of body-worn cameras statewide. At least 20 states have enacted laws that address state-level use-of-force standards.
The democratically elected D.C. government enacted common sense police reform three years ago. Congress should not overturn the will of District residents.
Robert Garcia,
Ranking Member.
